questions.q: The chapter calls the Ghaznavids a 'Turkic' power. What does the word 'Turkic' refer to?
o: Peoples, languages and cultures historically linked with a vast region stretching across Central Asia to Turkey and Siberia
Only the people living in present-day Turkey
The Arab rulers who had tried to invade north India in earlier centuries
Any army that entered India through the Khyber Pass
questions.a: Peoples, languages and cultures historically linked with a vast region stretching across Central Asia, all the way to Turkey and Siberia.

questions.q: Which city was the capital of the Ghaznavids?
questions.a: Ghazna, today's Ghazni in Afghanistan, which gave the Ghaznavids their name.

questions.q:
Match each person in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Jayapala  2. Anandapala  3. al-Utbi  4. Salar Masud
Column II: P. Mahmud's court historian who chronicled his campaigns  Q. Hindu Shahi ruler when the Ghaznavids overran the Shahis  R. Mahmud's nephew who, according to tradition, fell in battle at Bahraich  S. Jayapala's son, defeated by Mahmud in 1008 after a long battle
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Jayapala was the Hindu Shahi ruler when the Ghaznavids overran them; Anandapala was his son, defeated in 1008; al-Utbi was Mahmud's court historian; Salar Masud was Mahmud's nephew who fell at Bahraich.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Although Mahmud met strong resistance in India and was close to defeat on a few occasions, his campaigns were ultimately successful.
Reason (R): Mahmud's army depended mainly on slow-moving war elephants and foot soldiers.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the chapter says his large army's rapid marches and daring cavalry attacks, with archers on horseback, were ultimately decisive, not slow-moving elephants and foot soldiers.

questions.q: True or False? 'The Somnath temple that stands today was built in 1950 and was inaugurated the next year by Rajendra Prasad, the then President of India.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that after being rebuilt and destroyed several times, the existing Somanatha temple was built in 1950 and inaugurated the next year by President Rajendra Prasad, with its construction funded entirely from public donations.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives the reason: the chapter says the existing temple was built in 1950 and inaugurated in 1951 by President Rajendra Prasad

questions.q: (a) Who was Suheldev (or Suhaldev)? (b) What, according to oral history and a 17th-century chronicle, did he do?
questions.a: (a) Suheldev was the local ruler at Bahraich, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh. (b) Around the time of Mahmud's death, when Mahmud's nephew Salar Masud attacked the Gangetic region and reached Bahraich, Suheldev successfully resisted the attack and Salar Masud fell in the battle.
s: Identifies Suheldev as the local ruler at Bahraich in present-day Uttar Pradesh
States that he resisted Salar Masud's attack and Salar Masud fell in the battle

questions.q: The chapter shows a coin issued from Lahore by Mahmud (Fig. 4.9). (a) In which two languages was it written? (b) What did it call Mahmud, and what does that word mean? (c) Suggest one reason why a ruler whose capital was Ghazni would put Sanskrit on a coin issued at Lahore.
questions.a: (a) Arabic on one side and Sanskrit on the other. (b) It called him 'nripati', which means king (and it also praised Islam). (c) One acceptable reason: Lahore was in Punjab, the one part of India where Mahmud kept a base, so a Sanskrit side would help the coin be accepted by his Indian subjects there.
s: Names the two languages: Arabic and Sanskrit
States that it called Mahmud 'nripati', meaning king
Gives a sound reason linked to Punjab, such as helping the coin be accepted by his Indian subjects where Mahmud kept a base

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A museum in Gujarat has a panel on the year 1026. It reads: 'A few years after his raids on Mathura and Kannauj, Mahmud of Ghazni marched to Somnath in Saurashtra. After a few days of fighting he destroyed the Somanatha Shiva temple and looted its enormous treasures.' Beside the panel is a line from the scholar al-Biruni about what happened to the temple's image, and a photograph of the temple that stands at Somnath today, built in 1950.
(a) What kind of town was Somnath at that time, and how did its people meet Mahmud's attack?
(b) According to al-Biruni, what did Mahmud do with the image, and where did a part of it lie?
(c) About how many years after Mahmud's attack was the present temple built? Show the working.
(d) A visitor says, 'Mahmud attacked Somnath only for its treasure.' Using al-Biruni's record and what the chapter says about Mahmud's aims, judge this claim.
questions.a: (a) It was then a bustling seaport; the locals put up strong resistance and Mahmud's army suffered severe losses before he gained the upper hand after a few days of fighting. (b) He ordered the upper part to be broken and the rest to be taken to Ghazni; a part of it lay before the door of the mosque of Ghazni, where people rubbed their feet to clean them. (c) 1950 - 1026 = 924 years, so a little over nine centuries later. (d) The claim is too narrow: large temples held immense wealth from devotees' offerings, so plunder was a chief aim, but breaking the image and placing a part of it where people rub their feet, together with the chapter's evidence that Mahmud was keen to spread his version of Islam, show that his aims were religious as well as plunder.
s: Bustling seaport, with strong local resistance and severe losses to Mahmud's army
Upper part broken, the rest taken to Ghazni, a part lying before the door of the Ghazni mosque where people rubbed their feet
Works out 1950 - 1026 = 924 years
Judges the claim too narrow: plunder was a chief aim, but al-Biruni's record and Mahmud's wish to spread his version of Islam show a religious aim too

questions.q: Al-Biruni was a Persian scholar from Khwarizm. In which present-day country is Khwarizm?
questions.a: Uzbekistan; the chapter places Khwarizm in present-day Uzbekistan.

questions.q: What is Bhaskaracharya's Bijaganita mainly about?
questions.a: More advanced algebra; Lilavati teaches basic mathematics through riddles and Siddhantashiromani deals with astronomy.

questions.q: True or False? 'Bhaskaracharya wrote his most famous works in Persian, which is why they spread beyond India.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Bhaskaracharya's most famous works were all written in Sanskrit; several of them were translated into Persian later, during the Mughal period, which is how his influence spread.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: his works were in Sanskrit and were translated into Persian later, in the Mughal period

questions.q: (a) Name any two Indian mathematicians or astronomers whose work al-Biruni compiled. (b) In which two languages did al-Biruni write his works?
questions.a: (a) Any two of Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta. (b) Arabic and Persian.
s: Names two of Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta
Names Arabic and Persian

questions.q: A teacher wants to write a new Class 7 mathematics book that students will enjoy as much as they enjoyed Bhaskaracharya's works for centuries. Using the chapter, name three features of his writing she should copy, and explain how each one would help her students.
questions.a: (1) A gift for poetry: writing in an enjoyable, poetic way keeps students interested and makes the book pleasant to read. (2) Many examples, such as the lively riddles and problems of Lilavati: students learn an idea by working through a problem rather than memorising a rule. (3) Clear explanations, demonstrations and proofs: students can follow each step and check why a method works.
s: Poetry or enjoyable style, with how it keeps students interested
Examples, riddles or problems, with how they help students learn by doing
Clear explanations, demonstrations and proofs, with how they let students follow and check each step

questions.q: Al-Biruni's survey of India discussed Indian intellectual achievements 'as best he could, often comparing them with those of Greek and Islamic traditions'. What does this way of working show about his survey?
o: He set Indian learning beside other traditions he knew, treating it as a serious body of knowledge worth comparing
He wanted to prove that only Greek learning had any value
He compared India only with Greece, as he had never studied Islamic learning
He wrote the survey in Sanskrit so that Indian scholars could check it
questions.a: He set Indian learning beside the Greek and Islamic traditions he knew, treating it as a serious body of knowledge worth comparing.

questions.q: A student writes: 'After Mahmud's raids, Indian science declined everywhere in India, so no great Indian scientist worked in the 12th century.' Test her claim. (a) When and where was Bhaskaracharya born, according to the chapter? (b) What does the chapter say about his family, and what does this suggest about how learning was kept alive? (c) What exactly does the chapter say about the decline of scientific knowledge, and in which part of India? (d) Give your verdict on her claim, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) In 1114, probably in present-day Maharashtra. (b) His family counted several scholars and astronomers, which suggests that learning was passed on within families of scholars in regions away from the raids. (c) The production and transmission of scientific knowledge did decline in north India, a little later, but continued to flourish in other regions. (d) The claim is wrong: the decline was in north India, not everywhere, and Bhaskaracharya, one of India's greatest mathematicians and astronomers, was born in 1114 and did his great work in the 12th century outside the north.
s: 1114, probably in present-day Maharashtra
His family counted several scholars and astronomers, suggesting learning was passed on in families of scholars
Decline in north India a little later, while science continued to flourish in other regions
Rejects the claim: the decline was regional, and Bhaskaracharya worked in the 12th century outside the north

questions.q: After the decline of the Palas, the Senas became the dominant power over much of Bengal. Which city was their capital?
questions.a: Nadiya, now the Nadia district, which shares a border with Bangladesh.

questions.q: The poet Jayadeva, hosted by the Senas, wrote the famous Gitagovindam. Whose story does it tell?
questions.a: The story of Krishna and Radha.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Eastern Gangas began building the grand Sun temple at Konark in the mid-12th century.
Reason (R): By the end of the 12th century the Eastern Gangas had emerged as one of the most stable powers of eastern India.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: the chapter says the Eastern Gangas began the Konark Sun temple in the mid-13th century, not the mid-12th, and that by the end of the 12th century they were one of the most stable powers of eastern India.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about eastern India and the Deccan in this period.
I. The capital of the Western Chalukyas was Kalyani (or Kalyana).
II. The Sena capital Nadiya lies in today's Nadia district, which shares a border with Nepal.
III. At some point the rule of the Western Chalukyas extended to the Narmada River in the north.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the Nadia district shares a border with Bangladesh, not Nepal.

questions.q: Name the two famous temples whose construction was begun by the Eastern Gangas, and state where each stands.
questions.a: The Jagannatha temple at Puri and the grand Sun temple at Konark (begun in the mid-13th century).
s: Names the Jagannatha temple and states that it stands at Puri
Names the Sun temple and states that it stands at Konark

questions.q: Priya writes: 'The Senas of Bengal were brought down by their neighbours Kamarupa and Kalinga, with whom they were always at war.' (a) What does the chapter say about Sena relations with these two neighbours? (b) Who ended the Senas' control over much of Bengal, and how? (c) What happened to that same commander in Kamarupa in 1205, and what does this show about Priya's claim?
questions.a: (a) Relations with Kamarupa (Assam) and Kalinga (more or less present-day Odisha) seem to have alternated between friendly and conflictual, so they were not always at war. (b) Bakhtiyar Khilji, Aibak's army commander, caught the Sena ruler unaware at Nadiya around 1203-04. (c) The local ruler's forces inflicted severe losses on his army and the local people destroyed food and fodder, so he escaped with only a handful of men; far from bringing the Senas down, Kamarupa resisted the invader who ended them, so Priya's claim is wrong.
s: Relations alternated between friendly and conflictual, not always war
Bakhtiyar Khilji caught the Sena ruler unaware at Nadiya around 1203-04
Kamarupa inflicted severe losses on him (food and fodder destroyed, he escaped with a handful of men), so the claim is wrong

questions.q: While north India bore the brunt of the Ghaznavid raids, three other regions had their own stories. Describe the political scene in (a) Bengal, (b) Kalinga and (c) the Deccan in the 11th and 12th centuries, naming the dynasty and one key fact for each, plus (d) one cultural contribution from Bengal or Kalinga. (e) Then decide in which of the three regions the balance of power changed most, and give your reason.
questions.a: (a) Bengal: after the decline of the Palas, the Senas became the dominant power, with their capital at Nadiya, and their relations with Kamarupa and Kalinga alternated between friendly and conflictual. (b) Kalinga: the Eastern Gangas made marriage alliances with the Cholas but also clashed with them, and by the end of the 12th century were one of the most stable powers, ruling 'from the Ganga to the Godavari'. (c) Deccan: the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, once reaching the Narmada, fought fierce wars with the Cholas over Vengi. (d) The Senas promoted Hindu thought and hosted Jayadeva, author of the Gitagovindam; or the Eastern Gangas began the Jagannatha temple at Puri. (e) The Deccan changed most: the Western Chalukyas faded away and were replaced by the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas, while Kalinga stayed stable under the Eastern Gangas and Bengal passed from one dynasty to another (a well-argued choice of Bengal is also acceptable).
s: Bengal: Senas replace the Palas, capital Nadiya
Kalinga: Eastern Gangas, alliances and clashes with the Cholas, stable from the Ganga to the Godavari
Deccan: Western Chalukyas of Kalyani and the wars with the Cholas over Vengi
Gives one cultural contribution, such as Jayadeva's Gitagovindam or the Jagannatha temple at Puri
Decides which region changed most with a reason, such as the Western Chalukyas fading and being replaced by the Kakatiyas and Hoysalas

questions.q: According to the legend behind the Hoysala name, an ascetic called out 'Poy, Sala' when a tiger appeared. What do these words mean in old Kannada?
questions.a: Strike, Sala; Sala obeyed, saved the ascetic's life and was blessed with kingship.

questions.q:
Match each place of the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Orugallu  2. Velapura  3. Dvarasamudra  4. Hanamkonda
Column II: P. Today's Belur, a Hoysala capital  Q. Today's Warangal, the Kakatiya capital  R. Site of the Thousand Pillar temple  S. Today's Halebidu, a Hoysala capital
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Orugallu is today's Warangal, the Kakatiya capital; Velapura is Belur and Dvarasamudra is Halebidu, the Hoysala capitals; the Thousand Pillar temple stands at Hanamkonda.

questions.q: True or False? 'The Thousand Pillar temple, a fine example of Kakatiya temple architecture, stands inside the Kakatiya fort at Orugallu.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: False. The Thousand Pillar temple is at Hanamkonda; Orugallu (today's Warangal) was the Kakatiya capital, where they built a fort with impressive stone toranas or gateways.
s: States the verdict: False
Gives the reason: the Thousand Pillar temple is at Hanamkonda, while Orugallu (Warangal) was the capital with the fort

questions.q: The Hoysalas' most visible legacy is their temple architecture. (a) Name two features of the Hoysala style of temple building. (b) Name the two places whose Hoysala temples are particularly famous. (c) What recognition have these temples received?
questions.a: (a) Intricately carved stone pillars, and sculptures and carved panels. (b) Belur and Halebidu. (c) They are among three Hoysala temples recognised by UNESCO as world heritage monuments.
s: Names two features: intricately carved stone pillars, sculptures, panels
Names Belur and Halebidu
States that they are among three Hoysala temples recognised by UNESCO as world heritage monuments

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A Class 7 group in Hassan is making a heritage booklet on a dynasty of their region. Their notes say: the dynasty began in southern Karnataka; a legend recorded in its inscriptions tells how its founder, while at a Jain temple, struck at a tiger on an ascetic's command and saved the ascetic's life; under King Vishnuvardhana the kingdom stopped obeying its overlords, challenged a powerful dynasty of the Tamil country and gradually spread over most of present-day Karnataka; and its rule saw cultural and literary growth in the language of the region.
(a) Name the dynasty and its founder in the legend.
(b) From whose overlordship did it break away under Vishnuvardhana?
(c) Which powerful dynasty of the Tamil country did it challenge?
(d) In which language did its rule see cultural and literary development?
questions.a: (a) The Hoysalas; their founder was Sala. (b) The Chalukyas (Chalukya overlordship). (c) The Cholas. (d) Kannada.
s: Names the Hoysalas and their founder Sala
Chalukya overlordship
The Cholas
Kannada

questions.q: A traveller in the 12th century sets out from Orugallu and ends his journey at Dvarasamudra. (a) In which present-day city and state does he start and end, and which dynasty ruled each place? (b) Both these dynasties had grown at the expense of the same older Deccan power. Name it and say what weakened it.
questions.a: (a) He starts at Warangal in Telangana, the Kakatiya capital, and ends at Halebidu in Karnataka, a Hoysala capital. (b) The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani; they faded away after fierce wars with the Cholas over Vengi and the fertile region around it.
s: Warangal (Telangana) under the Kakatiyas and Halebidu (Karnataka) under the Hoysalas
Names the Western Chalukyas and the wars with the Cholas over Vengi that weakened them

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Kakatiyas and the Hoysalas.
I. The Hoysalas originated in southern Karnataka and, under King Vishnuvardhana, gradually extended their sway over most of present-day Karnataka.
II. The Kakatiya capital Orugallu and the Hoysala capital Velapura are today's Warangal and Halebidu.
III. The legend of the Hoysala name is mentioned in inscriptions and depicted in several temples.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: Orugallu is Warangal, but Velapura is today's Belur; Halebidu was Dvarasamudra.

questions.q: Which temple did Rajaraja Chola build at Thanjavur?
o: The Brihadishvara temple, also called Rajarajeshvaram
questions.a: The Brihadishvara temple, also known as Rajarajeshvaram after Rajaraja, a masterpiece of architecture and engineering.

questions.q: Rajendra Chola I took the title 'Gangaikondachola'. What does this title mean?
o: The Chola who seized (or brought) the Ganga
The Chola who ruled the seas
The Chola who conquered Sri Lanka
The Chola who built the great temple
questions.a: The Chola who seized (or brought) the Ganga, recalling his campaigns in the north and the sacredness of the Ganga.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After Rajendra Chola I's campaigns, northern Sri Lanka remained a part of the Chola Empire for all the following centuries.
Reason (R): Rajendra expanded his father Rajaraja's conquest of northern Sri Lanka.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: Rajendra did expand his father's conquest, but northern Sri Lanka stayed in the Chola Empire only for half a century or so, until King Vijayabahu I drove the Cholas out.

questions.q: (a) In which present-day state did the Cholas rise to prominence? (b) Name the three capital cities of the Cholas given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Present-day Tamil Nadu. (b) Tanjavur (present-day Thanjavur), Gangaikondacholapuram and Kanchi (present-day Kanchipuram).
s: Present-day Tamil Nadu
Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram and Kanchi (Kanchipuram)

questions.q: Chola kings supported several religious buildings. (a) What is the other name of the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur, and after whom is it named? (b) What does the temple Rajendra Chola I built at Gangaikondacholapuram commemorate? (c) The Cholas were predominantly Shaivites, yet Rajaraja facilitated the building of a Buddhist vihara at Nagapattinam by the ruler of the Srivijaya Empire. Using (a), (b) and (c), suggest two purposes, besides worship, for which Chola kings supported religious buildings.
questions.a: (a) Rajarajeshvaram, named after Rajaraja. (b) Rajendra's victory over north Indian rulers. (c) To make the king's own name and fame last (Rajarajeshvaram) or to record his victories (Gangaikondacholapuram), and to build good relations with a foreign ruler and his followers, as with the vihara for the Srivijaya ruler at a Chola port.
s: Rajarajeshvaram, named after Rajaraja
Commemorates Rajendra's victory over north Indian rulers
Suggests two purposes: honouring the king or recording victories, and building ties with a foreign ruler

questions.q: Imagine you are a scribe at the Chola court at Gangaikondacholapuram during the reign of Rajendra Chola I (1014-44). Write four short diary entries, each based on a different fact from the chapter, about: (a) the king's campaigns in the north and the title he took; (b) the trade with China; (c) the public works the Cholas carry out at home; (d) the war in Sri Lanka.
questions.a: (a) 'The king has returned from conquering parts of Odisha and Bengal and now calls himself Gangaikondachola, the Chola who brought the Ganga.' (b) 'Our merchants' ships trade with China, and the king has even sent a diplomatic mission there.' (c) 'New roads make travel to the inland towns easier, and tanks, wells, canals and artificial lakes water the fields of the kingdom.' (d) 'The king has extended his father's conquest of northern Sri Lanka, which is now part of our empire.'
s: Entry on the northern campaigns in Odisha and Bengal and the title Gangaikondachola
Entry on the thriving China trade or the diplomatic mission to China
Entry on Chola public works: roads, or tanks, wells and canals for irrigation, or artificial lakes
Entry on extending the conquest of northern Sri Lanka

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In 1025 a large Chola fleet sailed east across the Bay of Bengal against a kingdom that controlled one of the sea routes used in the Chola trade with China. Many Indian merchant guilds supported the voyage. Under the Cholas this trade thrived, as archaeological evidence and inscriptions confirm, and the king had even sent a diplomatic mission to China. The chapter says that the expedition 'seems to have achieved its objectives'.
(a) Which Chola king sent this fleet, and against which empire?
(b) In which present-day countries did that empire lie?
(c) Why would merchant guilds support a naval war?
(d) What did the Chola navy achieve, and how would this outcome have served the guilds?
questions.a: (a) Rajendra Chola I, against the Srivijaya Empire. (b) In parts of present-day Malaysia and Indonesia. (c) Their ships carried the thriving trade with China, and the Srivijaya king's control of one of the sea routes created competition with the Cholas, so punishing him protected their trade. (d) It defeated the Srivijaya forces and captured their capital; with the rival punished, the guilds' trade along the route to China was safer, which is the objective the chapter says was achieved.
s: Rajendra Chola I, against the Srivijaya Empire
Parts of present-day Malaysia and Indonesia
Guilds' China trade faced competition from the Srivijaya king's control of a sea route, so they backed the punishment
Navy defeated the Srivijaya forces and captured the capital, making the guilds' trade route safer

questions.q: 'The wars that made the Cholas great also brought them down.' Evaluate this statement. Give two Chola gains from war or naval power, one sign of strong rule at home, two ways their conflicts weakened them, and end with your judgement.
questions.a: Gains: Rajaraja conquered parts of Karnataka and Andhra, the 'islands of the sea' (the Maldives) and northern Sri Lanka including Anuradhapura; Rajendra conquered parts of Odisha and Bengal and defeated Srivijaya, protecting the China trade. Strong rule at home: the Cholas built roads, tanks, wells, canals and artificial lakes. Weakening: frequent and extensive conflicts with the Western Chalukyas, the Pandyas and the rulers of Sri Lanka drained the treasury; Sri Lanka was lost when Vijayabahu I drove the Cholas out. Judgement: the statement is largely true, since by the 13th century the empire had shrunk and was absorbed by the Pandyas after these drawn-out wars.
s: Gives a first gain, such as Rajaraja's conquests including the Maldives or northern Sri Lanka
Gives a second gain, such as Rajendra's conquest of Odisha and Bengal or the Srivijaya victory
Names public works at home: roads, tanks, wells, canals, artificial lakes
Explains two weakening effects: wars with the Western Chalukyas, Pandyas and Sri Lanka drained the treasury; Sri Lanka was lost to Vijayabahu I
Gives a judgement supported by the end of the empire: shrunk by the 13th century and absorbed by the Pandyas

questions.q: In which region did the Paramaras emerge as an independent power in the second half of the 10th century?
o: The Konkan coast, in present-day Maharashtra
questions.a: Malwa, a region in present-day Madhya Pradesh, with Dhara (present-day Dhar) as the capital.

questions.q: The name of the city of Bhopal comes from 'Bhojpal'. What does 'Bhojpal' mean?
o: The dam or fort of Bhoja
questions.a: The 'dam' or 'fort of Bhoja', recalling the vast lake Bhoja built near the city.

questions.q: (a) Name Bhoja Paramara's long treatise on architecture. (b) Give any two subjects it deals with.
questions.a: (a) Samarangana Sutradhara. (b) Any two of: architecture, town planning, temple construction, sculpture, mechanical devices.
s: Names the Samarangana Sutradhara
Gives two subjects, such as town planning and temple construction

questions.q: True or False? 'Before they emerged as an independent power in Malwa, the Paramaras had been vassals of the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the Paramaras were originally vassals of the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas, and emerged as an independent power in Malwa in the second half of the 10th century, with Dhara as their capital.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: they were originally vassals of the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas before becoming independent in Malwa in the second half of the 10th century

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Under Bhoja, the Paramara capital became a renowned centre of learning that attracted scholars, poets and artists from across India.
Reason (R): Bhoja constructed a vast lake between Bhojpur and Bhopal by harnessing the waters of several rivers.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the chapter links the centre of learning to Bhoja's generous patronage of scholars and of Sanskrit literature, under which arts and sciences flourished; the lake was a public work for irrigation and water management.

questions.q: A visitor at the Bhojeshwar temple says, 'Bhoja must have been a weak king. His temple was never finished and his dynasty fell soon after him.' Examine her claim. (a) What does the chapter say about the Bhojeshwar temple even though it was never completed? (b) Give two facts from the chapter that show Bhoja was a strong ruler. (c) What does the chapter say caused the Paramaras' decline, and does it blame Bhoja?
questions.a: (a) It remains an architectural marvel, so an unfinished temple is not proof of a weak king. (b) Any two: he ruled from 1010 for almost half a century; he led numerous campaigns extending his kingdom from the Konkan to parts of Rajasthan; he sent forces to help the Hindu Shahis against Mahmud; he was known for efficient governance and public works such as the vast lake near Bhopal. (c) After his death in 1055 the Paramaras declined gradually, partly because of conflicts with neighbouring powers; the chapter does not blame Bhoja, so the claim is weak.
s: States that the temple remains an architectural marvel even though unfinished, so it does not prove weakness
Gives two facts showing strength, such as campaigns from the Konkan to Rajasthan or efficient governance and public works
States the decline came after his death, partly from conflicts with neighbours, so the chapter does not blame him

questions.q: In a class debate, Team A says, 'Bhoja Paramara should be remembered mainly as a warrior king,' and Team B says, 'He should be remembered mainly as a scholar.' Using the chapter: (a) give two facts that support Team A; (b) name three kinds of works that Bhoja himself wrote; (c) state what the chapter says about his reputation in later times; (d) decide which team the chapter supports more strongly, and give your reason.
questions.a: (a) Any two: he ruled from 1010 for almost half a century; he led numerous campaigns that extended his kingdom from the Konkan region on the west coast to parts of Rajasthan; he sent forces to help the Hindu Shahi rulers against Mahmud of Ghazni. (b) Any three: the Samarangana Sutradhara, a long treatise on architecture, town planning, temple construction, sculpture and mechanical devices; treatises on governance; a treatise on Sanskrit poetics; a commentary on Patanjali's Yogasutras; texts of medicine. (c) His reputation as a wise and learned ruler became legendary and inspired numerous stories and folk tales. (d) Team B: both sides hold facts, but the chapter calls him 'the scholar-king', gives his learning and writings far more space than his campaigns, and says it is his wisdom and learning that became legendary.
s: Two facts for Team A: long reign, campaigns from the Konkan to Rajasthan, or help to the Hindu Shahis
Three kinds of works: the Samarangana Sutradhara, governance, poetics, the Yogasutras commentary, medicine
His reputation as wise and learned became legendary, with many stories and folk tales
Decides for Team B with a reason from the chapter, such as the title 'scholar-king' and his legendary reputation for learning

questions.q: Where is Tarain, the site of the battles between Prithviraj III and Muhammad Ghuri, today?
questions.a: Tarain is modern-day Taraori in Haryana.

questions.q: Which of Muhammad Ghuri's generals, left behind in India to consolidate his gains, later founded the Delhi Sultanate?
questions.a: Qutb-ud-din Aibak, his most notable general, later founded the Delhi Sultanate.

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) Where was Ghur, the home of the Ghurids? (b) Which Chaulukya king defeated Muhammad Ghuri at the foot of Mount Abu in 1178? (c) What was the capital of the Chahamanas, and what is it called today?
questions.a: (a) Ghur (present-day Ghor) was a mountainous region in Afghanistan, to the west of Ghazni. (b) Mularaja II (another version credits his mother, Queen Naikidevi). (c) Ajayameru, today's Ajmer.
s: Ghur: a mountainous region of Afghanistan west of Ghazni
Mularaja II (or Queen Naikidevi in another version)
Ajayameru, today's Ajmer

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Ghurids.
I. The chiefs of Ghur had earlier been vassals of the Ghaznavids.
II. Muhammad Ghuri's formal name, found on his gold coin, was Muhammad ibn Sam.
III. Bakhtiyar Khilji was killed in battle by the forces of the ruler of Kamarupa in 1205.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: Bakhtiyar escaped from Kamarupa with a handful of men and was assassinated in 1206, apparently by his own men.

questions.q: A historian says the Ghurids first rose to power 'by taking advantage of a neighbour's weakness'. Which fact from the chapter fits this description best?
o: After Mahmud, the Ghaznavid Empire came under attack from several sides and broke up, and the chiefs of Ghur, earlier its vassals, seized the chance to take Ghazni
Muhammad Ghuri defeated Prithviraj III at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191
The Chaulukya king Mularaja II invited Muhammad Ghuri into Gujarat in 1178
Bakhtiyar Khilji captured Ghazni from the Hindu Shahis
questions.a: After Mahmud, the Ghaznavid Empire came under attack from several sides and disintegrated, and the chiefs of Ghur, earlier its vassals, seized the opportunity to take control of Ghazni and build up their power.

questions.q: True or False? 'Delhi was part of the Chahamana empire, and it was after defeating the Chahamana king at the Second Battle of Tarain that Muhammad Ghuri went on to capture it.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. In the 12th century the Chahamanas conquered Delhi, Haryana, parts of Punjab and Uttar Pradesh as well as most of Rajasthan; after defeating and executing Prithviraj III at the Second Battle of Tarain, Muhammad Ghuri went on to capture Delhi.
s: States the verdict: True
Links the two facts: Delhi was among the Chahamana conquests, and Muhammad captured it after defeating Prithviraj III at the Second Battle of Tarain

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Nalanda Mahavihara in Bihar drew learners from many lands. The Chinese pilgrims Yijing and Xuanzang spent time there studying manuscripts. A ruler of the Srivijaya Empire made donations to Nalanda and asked the Pala king for land to build one more monastery there. Tibetan scholars both taught and studied at Nalanda. Near the end of the 12th century an army commander of the Ghurids, on his way to Bengal, destroyed it.
(a) What did Yijing and Xuanzang take back to China from Nalanda?
(b) Was the Srivijaya ruler's request granted, and how do we know?
(c) Name the commander who destroyed Nalanda and one other Buddhist university he destroyed.
(d) Using the passage, explain why the destruction of Nalanda was a loss for other lands of Asia as well as for India.
questions.a: (a) Many manuscripts, which they had selected while studying there. (b) Yes; a copper-plate found at Nalanda records that the request was granted. (c) Bakhtiyar Khilji; Vikramashila. (d) Scholars and rulers from China, Tibet and the Srivijaya Empire studied, taught or gave gifts there, so Nalanda was a shared centre of learning for many lands; its loss cut them off from it, and Tibetan scholars had to flee.
s: Many manuscripts they had selected
Yes, recorded on a copper-plate found at Nalanda
Bakhtiyar Khilji; Vikramashila
Explains Nalanda served learners from China, Tibet and Srivijaya, so its loss was shared

questions.q: In 1178 Muhammad Ghuri was defeated in Gujarat, yet by 1206 his generals held territory across north India. Trace how this change came about in five steps, giving the date or place of each, and work out about how many years passed between Bakhtiyar Khilji's capture of Nadiya (around 1203-04) and Muhammad's death in 1206.
questions.a: (1) 1178: defeated by the Chaulukya king Mularaja II at the foot of Mount Abu, so his push into Gujarat failed. (2) 1191: defeated by Prithviraj III at Tarain, but returned within a year with a larger army. (3) 1192: won the Second Battle of Tarain and executed Prithviraj. (4) He captured Delhi and, unlike Mahmud, sought territorial conquest, leaving commanders such as Qutb-ud-din Aibak to consolidate his gains. (5) Aibak's commander Bakhtiyar Khilji conquered Bihar and Bengal, ending Sena control at Nadiya around 1203-04; Muhammad was killed in 1206, only about two to three years later (1206 - 1204 = 2, 1206 - 1203 = 3), and the territory stayed under his generals.
s: 1178 defeat at Mount Abu by Mularaja II
1191 defeat at Tarain and return with a larger army
1192 victory at the Second Battle of Tarain, Prithviraj executed
Capture of Delhi and generals such as Aibak left to hold the gains
Bakhtiyar's conquest of Bihar and Bengal (Nadiya, 1203-04), about two to three years before Muhammad's death in 1206, and the generals keeping control

questions.q: Which king built the Angkor Wat temple in Cambodia in the 12th century?
questions.a: The Khmer king Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat in the 12th century.

questions.q: What were Basavanna's vachanas?
o: Short poems in Kannada conveying his spiritual and ethical vision
questions.a: Short poems in Kannada that convey his spiritual and ethical vision and his devotion to his Lord.

questions.q:
Your class is making a chart called 'Five achievements of the 11th and 12th centuries'. For each item, write who made or founded it and one fact about it.
(a) Lilavati
(b) Kandariya Mahadeva temple
(c) Gitagovindam
(d) Lingayat movement
(e) Bhojeshwar temple
questions.a: (a) Bhaskaracharya; it uses lively riddles and problems to teach basic mathematics. (b) The Chandellas; one of dozens of temples built at Khajuraho. (c) The poet Jayadeva, hosted by the Senas; it tells the story of Krishna and Radha. (d) Basavanna (Basaveshwara); it rejected caste distinctions and ritualism and taught personal devotion and dedicated work. (e) Bhoja Paramara; it remains an architectural marvel even though it was never completed.
s: Lilavati: Bhaskaracharya, with one fact
Kandariya Mahadeva: the Chandellas at Khajuraho
Gitagovindam: Jayadeva (hosted by the Senas), with one fact
Lingayat movement: Basavanna, with one fact
Bhojeshwar temple: Bhoja Paramara, with one fact

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many rulers of this period took care of irrigation works.
Reason (R): Irrigation could, to some extent, reduce the effects of uncertain seasonal rains on farming, the mainstay of the economy.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: agriculture was the mainstay of the economy, and irrigation helped protect it from the vagaries of seasonal rains.

questions.q: A museum label beside a photograph of Angkor Wat asks how Indian religious and artistic ideas reached a Khmer kingdom far across the sea. Which answer does the chapter's 'Taking Stock' support?
o: External trade was a vehicle for the spread of Indian culture in Southeast Asia and China
Indian kings conquered Cambodia and ruled it for two centuries
The Turkic invaders carried Indian ideas east after their raids
Khmer kings settled in India and later returned home
questions.a: External trade was a vehicle for the spread of Indian culture in Southeast Asia and China; internal and external trade continued and the merchant guilds survived and adapted.

questions.q: The chapter says the lesson of the period, if there is one, is 'resilience'. Give two reasons from the chapter that support this lesson.
questions.a: Any two: large parts of northern India and all of south India remained outside the hold of the Turkic invaders; trade inside India and abroad continued and the merchant guilds survived and adapted; cultural traditions persisted, with new schools of thought and literary and scientific works in Sanskrit and regional languages.
s: First reason, such as much of India staying outside Turkic rule
Second reason, such as trade and guilds surviving or culture and learning continuing

questions.q: Arjun writes, 'By the end of the 12th century, all of India had come under Turkic rule, and Indian kings never united against invaders.' Point out the two errors in his statement, and give one example of an Indian ruler who sent help against an invader.
questions.a: Error 1: large parts of northern India and all of south India remained outside the hold of the Turkic invaders. Error 2: on a few occasions native rulers came together to form a coalition against a foreign invader, and alliances were not uncommon. Example: Bhoja Paramara sent forces to help the Hindu Shahi rulers against Mahmud of Ghazni.
s: Corrects the first error: much of north India and all of south India stayed outside Turkic rule
Corrects the second error: native rulers sometimes formed coalitions against a foreign invader
Example: Bhoja Paramara helping the Hindu Shahis against Mahmud

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A museum displays finds from a west-coast port site of the 11th and 12th centuries: coins and pottery from China and Southeast Asia, timbers from a shipyard where seafaring ships were built, and large storage jars that once held raw cotton waiting to be loaded. A copy of an old record shows a king's officer collecting a tax from the merchants of the port.
(a) Which finds show trade with China and Southeast Asia?
(b) According to the chapter, from which regions of India did cotton come?
(c) According to the chapter, who supported the brisk trade of this period?
(d) A visitor says, 'Kings of this period cared only about war, not about the trade of ports.' Do you agree? Use the chapter to give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) The coins and pottery from China and Southeast Asia. (b) Western India and the Deccan. (c) A few powerful merchant guilds. (d) No: because of constant warfare every powerful king needed a sizable army, with soldiers, weapons, horses and elephants (and camels in parts of the north), which took considerable resources; so kingdoms needed an efficient administration to collect tributes from vassals and taxes from traders, and the trade of ports helped pay for the wars.
s: Names the Chinese and Southeast Asian coins and pottery
Western India and the Deccan
A few powerful guilds
Disagrees: a sizable army needed large resources, so kings needed efficient administration to collect taxes from traders
